newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - India struggles to preserve Gandhi legacy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - India struggles to preserve Gandhi legacy.

text.p: His statue can be found in almost every Indian village. Every town has at least one street named after him. His message of non-violence and uprightness is taught in every school.

But as India celebrates its 50th year as an independent nation, many believe that Mahatma Gandhi, its spiritual founding father, is now more of a political token than a role model in the nation he led to freedom from British rule in 1947.

Born on October 2, 1869, Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, popularly called Mahatma or the Great Soul, fell to a Hindu fanatic's bullets in 1948, five months after India became independent. Gandhi was a great preacher of Hindu-Moslem unity.

His decades-long non-violent movement has inspired leaders like exiled Tibetan leader Dalai Lama and Nelson Mandela, who led a movement against apartheid policies of racial segregation in South Africa.
But in India, his followers say that the values he stood for are under assault.

Gandhi preached non-violence but political violence is common in India. Gandhi's economic dream of self-sufficient villages has been replaced by a quest for global links and high technology that critics say throw people out of jobs.
Gandhi believed in austere living, but his followers are worried about increasing consumerism in India.

Gandhi often defied authorities wilfully to court arrest and uphold the principles he stood for. But leaders of the Congress party, which Gandhi controlled for years, have been busy moving bail applications in corruption cases.
"The Congress says it has the legacy of Gandhi. But they have slaughtered it so many times," economist L.C. Jain, a staunch follower of Gandhi, told Reuters.
When Congress, its leader mired in a corruption scandal, needed to choose a new chief last month, eyes turned to a disciple of Mahatma Gandhi.

"They have realised that only the Gandhi cap can give them salvation," Sitaram Kesri, a Gandhi follower who was imprisoned during the freedom movement, told Reuters after being tapped to replace former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.
Rao resigned as party chief following a court summons in a criminal conspiracy case.
"Let me tell you. I have to fight it out. We have to fight corruption at every level," Kesri said.

Kesri said decades in power had changed the party, but added that the Congress, which has ruled India for all but four years since independence, could still come back despite its worst electoral debacle this year with help from right people.
"Even today, 16,000 freedom fighters get out to campaign for us because of Mahatma Gandhi's memories," Kesri said.
"The moment they (Congress workers) remember the tears of the poor, people will rally around."
Kesri said Gandhi's legacy survives, pointing to India's existence as the world's largest democracy for 50 years. Congress, he said, also followed Gandhi's economic values in its own way.
"If you go through his articles, he has pleaded for small industries and cottage industries, and the government has all along been giving priority to this," Kesri said.
Kesri defended India's five-year-old economic reform programme, which critics say is at odds with Gandhian principles of self-reliance and small industries.
He said even global giants supported small ancillaries that provided jobs to poor people.
But critics like Jain say that today's police control of crowds was anathema to Gandhi, who believed in the power of commoners and social reformers like himself, not the state apparatus.

Economic reforms now put people last, not first, Jain said. "Now they are talking of a human face in economics. Gandhi had the whole human body in mind. If somebody had mentioned human face in his presence, he would have revolted."

Jain said Gandhian values are not common among politicians, but in society he said they can be found in the non-violent protests led by environmental campaigners and women's groups campaigning against prohibition.
"It (Gandhian change) is not coming through the state, it is coming through the society," Jain said.

Gandhian thinkers are also cheering a recent constitutional amendment which has made elections to village councils, called panchayats, mandatory, with a third of the seats reserved for women. There will also be quotas for low castes.
"Its (village self-rule's) importance in reconstructing politics cannot be minimised," Jain said.
